blocks.text: SESSION 1 — Concept · Key Points · Memory Technique. Read, absorb, stop.
1. Concept Explained Simply

Every architecture programme reaches a point where more than one valid way forward exists. Architecture Alternatives and Trade-offs is TOGAF's formal technique for handling this: when multiple Target Architectures could all validly conform to the Vision, Principles, and Requirements, how do you identify options, compare them honestly, and make a governed decision?

The technique matters for three reasons beyond simply choosing: it surfaces hidden agendas (stakeholders reveal real priorities when shown explicit trade-offs), it surfaces hidden requirements (reactions to alternatives reveal undocumented constraints), and it creates a governed decision trail (a documented rationale that survives scrutiny years later).
2. Key Points

The concept: There is often more than one possible Target Architecture that would conform to the Architecture Vision, Principles, and Requirements. Presenting alternatives and trade-offs to stakeholders helps architects extract hidden agendas, principles, and requirements that could impact the final Target Architecture.
The three-part Trade-off Method:

rows: Use Architecture Vision, Principles, Requirements, and stakeholder concerns to establish evaluation criteria
For each: define overview criteria, describe the architecture, estimate gaps from baseline, understand impacts across the Architecture Landscape
Choose one alternative, or combine features from multiple into a proposed hybrid

blocks.text: Applies at: Any phase in the ADM, any level of the architecture (Strategic/Segment/Capability), and per domain — with per-domain alternatives mergeable into a whole-architecture analysis.

Typical criteria: Flexibility · Time and cost of realisation (including transitions and "islands of stability") · Time period over which benefits are achieved · Adherence to architecture styles/guidelines · Solution delivery method (re-use, develop, buy) · Minimal impact on business capabilities during implementation · Minimised risk.

Step 4 of Part 2 — impacts and trade-offs: For each alternative, identify impact on any existing architectures and Transition Architectures within the Architecture Landscape, and impact on any running or planned implementation projects.

Relationship to Architecture Principles: Criteria must include the Architecture Principles. An alternative that is cheaper/faster but violates a principle is not automatically valid — it requires a formal governance decision (exception or principle revision), not an informal workaround.
3. Memory Technique

The three-part method — "CDC": Criteria → Describe alternatives → Choose or Combine.

The forcing-function insight: Presenting alternatives with explicit trade-offs forces stakeholders to reveal what they actually prioritise — not what they said in the abstract.

EXAM TRAP 1 — APPLIED PER DOMAIN, THEN MERGED. Alternatives are typically evaluated per domain (Application Architecture separately from Technology Architecture) to simplify analysis, then merged into a whole-architecture view. Not one set of alternatives immediately for the whole architecture.

EXAM TRAP 2 — NON-COMPLIANT ALTERNATIVES ARE NOT AUTOMATICALLY DISQUALIFIED. An alternative violating a principle may prompt the Architecture Board to reconsider the principle — but this requires formal governance, not an informal workaround.
EXAM TRAP 3 — APPLIES AT ANY PHASE, NOT JUST PHASE E. The technique feeds into Phase E's roadmap consolidation but is performed wherever significant architectural decisions arise throughout the ADM.
EXAM TRAP 4 — THE ARCHITECT PROPOSES; THE ARCHITECTURE BOARD SELECTS. Consistent with all major TOGAF governance decisions: the EA does the analysis, the governance body makes the call.
✋ PAUSE POINT — CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING. Answer from memory before reading Session 2.
1. What are the three parts of the Architecture Trade-off Method?

Part 1 — Define Criteria (from Vision, Principles, Requirements, stakeholder concerns). Part 2 — Identify and Describe Alternatives (criteria, architecture description, gap estimate, Landscape impacts). Part 3 — Select or Combine (choose one or merge features into a hybrid).
2. Why does presenting alternatives help "extract hidden agendas, principles, and requirements"?

Explicit trade-offs force stakeholders to reveal what they actually prioritise — a stakeholder who says "I want the best solution" reveals real priorities when shown Alternative A costs $2M more but delivers twice as fast. This surfaces constraints never formally articulated.
3. At which ADM phases and levels can this technique be applied?
Any phase in the ADM and any level of the architecture (Strategic, Segment, Capability) — not limited to Phase E.
SESSION 2 — Real-World Example · How It Works in Practice · Practice Questions · Part 2 Scenario
4. Real-World Example — GlobalTech Dynamics 365

**Phase D integration layer decision** — three alternatives evaluated: Alt 1: Azure API Management (high principle adherence, fast, managed service, Microsoft vendor dependency) · Alt 2: Self-hosted MuleSoft on Azure IaaS (maximum flexibility, high operational burden, longer implementation, lower vendor dependency) · Alt 3: Direct REST connections (cheapest, fastest, but violates the "approved middleware only" principle).

**Hidden requirement surfaced**: When shown Alternative 2, the Head of IT Operations reveals a previously undisclosed concern about Microsoft vendor lock-in. This surfaces a new criterion: "minimise vendor concentration risk."

**Architecture Board decision**: Alternative 3 eliminated as non-compliant. Alternative 1 selected for principle alignment, skills fit, and timeline — but the vendor concentration concern is formalised as a new Architecture Principle: "No single vendor shall provide more than 60% of enterprise middleware capability." Full rationale documented in the Architecture Repository for future reference.
5. How It Actually Works in Practice

REALITY CHECK: MOST ORGANISATIONS SKIP THIS AND PAY FOR IT LATER. Technology decisions are frequently made informally — "the infra team knows Azure." Without a documented trade-off analysis, the decision has no defensible rationale when challenged years later.

REALITY CHECK: CRITERIA MUST BE AGREED BEFORE ALTERNATIVES ARE SHOWN. If stakeholders see alternatives first, they unconsciously define criteria that favour their preferred option. Criteria come from Vision, Principles, and Requirements — established before anyone knows which alternative they'll favour.
6. Part 1 Practice Questions
Q1. Which best describes the primary purpose of the Architecture Alternatives and Trade-offs technique?

items: A) To identify the cheapest and fastest Target Architecture
B) To identify alternative Target Architectures conforming to Vision, Principles, and Requirements, and understand trade-offs to support a governed decision ✓
C) To allow project teams to select their preferred technology without Board involvement
D) To document why the initially proposed architecture was rejected

blocks.text: Answer: B — the Architecture Board makes the final selection, not project teams; the goal is governed decision-making, not cost minimisation.
Q2. At what point should evaluation criteria be defined?

items: A) After all alternatives are described, tailored to distinguish them
B) Before alternatives are identified — derived from Vision, Principles, Requirements, stakeholder concerns ✓
C) During Phase E when the roadmap is finalised
D) By the Architecture Board at the point of decision

blocks.text: Answer: B — defining criteria after alternatives are known allows unconscious bias to shape the evaluation.
Q3. An alternative — direct REST connections — clearly violates "all integrations must use approved middleware." How should the architect handle this?

items: A) Exclude it — only compliant alternatives should be presented
B) Include it — presenting a non-compliant alternative makes the cost of the principle visible and may prompt the Board to reaffirm or reconsider it ✓
C) Apply for a Dispensation before including it
D) Include it only if formally requested by the project team

blocks.text: Answer: B — including non-compliant alternatives deliberately makes trade-offs visible. The decision remains with the Architecture Board.
7. Part 2 Scenario Question (Exam-Authentic Format)

SCENARIO: Three cloud platform alternatives are analysed: Azure (aligns with Dynamics 365, familiar, highest vendor concentration risk), AWS (lowest unit cost, highest integration complexity), Hybrid (lowest vendor risk, highest operational complexity). The CFO says: "We're already on Azure — this analysis is just extra work. Can we just document the Azure decision and move on?"

rows: Agree — Azure is obviously right, alternatives analysis is redundant. This is exactly how organisations end up with undocumented, ungoverned decisions that cause problems years later.

Partially agree — if Azure clearly aligns, the analysis can be abbreviated: document criteria, confirm Azure meets them, briefly note why others weren't selected. Pragmatic and TOGAF-aligned ("just enough detail"), but loses marks for not acknowledging the hidden requirement (vendor concentration risk) already surfaced.

Disagree — all three alternatives require full architecture views and impact assessments regardless. Over-rigid; TOGAF explicitly allows proportionate depth ("just enough detail to support the decision").

Disagree with the CFO's characterisation — the analysis already surfaced a significant hidden concern (vendor concentration risk) not captured in the Vision or Principles. Even if Azure is selected, the analysis produced real value: a new Architecture Principle proposal and documented rationale. Complete to the level needed for a governed Board decision — not a bilateral CFO/EA agreement. Best answer.
